title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for short-stay turnover
audience: Owners of short-stay turnover businesses who want more work from hosts and managers who run holiday rentals and serviced apartments in their service area.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need.
Identify public signals that a client need is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily.

instruction.heading: Decide what work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Write down the property types you turn over well (for example, two-bedroom apartments in one precinct), the price range you can sustain, the suburbs you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each host books. A host with several properties close together, and a steady booking pattern, is worth far more than one isolated property. Business.gov.au suggests writing one profile for each customer segment (24 September 2024).

instruction.heading: Build a scored list of hosts and managers
instruction.body: Keep one list with a fit column and a status column. Score each prospect as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, using the criteria. Ask whether the host sits inside your service area, whether the booking pattern gives a repeat need, whether you can reach the person who makes the decision, and whether the work falls inside your insurance. Record the date and source of each contact detail. Do not buy or scrape lists, because ACMA says buying a list does not remove the duty to show consent.

instruction.heading: Use public signals for businesses, not for private hosts
instruction.body: Councils may publish accommodation registers, and the City of Port Phillip is one example named in the research. That register was not checked in detail, so check your own council. A planning permit register can show new dwellings at application stage, but it does not show whether they will be short-stay. If a signal concerns a private person rather than a business, leave it alone. Do not use private information about any individual to make contact.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A first message says how you found the host or manager, makes one observation you can verify from their public listing or service range, and offers one small next step, such as a turnover quote for one property with a checklist. Keep it honest and short. The ACCC found in July 2026 that many unsolicited approaches were pressured or misleading, and that many salespeople did not identify themselves (ACCC, 28 July 2026). Identify yourself and make it easy to decline.

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide the number of follow-ups and the gap between them in advance. Remove any host or manager who says no or asks you to stop, and record the request. ACMA says an unsubscribe must be honoured within five working days. Each month, review which fit tier and which signal produced paid work.

procedure: Write the property types, area, price range and booking-pattern criteria for the work you want.
Build the list, score each host or manager as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, and record the source of each contact detail.
Choose the public signals to check, and note the date each one is checked.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules, the Do Not Call Register and your insurance before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of each month.

workedExamples.situation: [ILLUSTRATIVE] A solo cleaner covers three inner suburbs of Melbourne. A property manager there runs eight short-stay apartments in one building, and its general contact email is on its website. The cleaner has not worked for the manager before.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the cleaner send a sales message to the manager now, and what should it contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: The manager is a business that runs several properties inside the service area, so it is a strong fit on the criteria. The cleaner does not send a sales email just because the address is published. ACMA says publishing a business address does not by itself permit commercial messages, so the cleaner first checks whether the manager has agreed to receive messages or has invited contact. If not, the cleaner checks the Do Not Call Register before any phone call, and calls only within the DNCR guide's hours (weekdays 9am to 8pm and Saturdays 9am to 5pm; 2018 guide). The first message names the building's public listing, says how the business learned of it, offers a turnover quote for one apartment with a checklist, and asks one question. The cleaner does not contact any guest or any private host.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to every host on a broad list.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong fits.

commonErrors.error: Using guest or private-host information to make contact.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person gave you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Pitching a service you are not insured to deliver.
commonErrors.prevention: Check insurance before outreach. Licence and insurance rules for turnover cleaning were not researched.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop.
commonErrors.prevention: Fix a number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This lesson does not grant any licence. Licence and insurance rules for turnover cleaning were not researched, and council registration for short-stay accommodation varies. Check the rule for each state or territory and council where you work.

Commercial electronic messages are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA says marketing messages need consent, that consent must be recorded, and that an unsubscribe must be honoured within five working days. The Act's text was not read for this lesson.
Check every telephone number against the Do Not Call Register before a telemarketing call. The 2018 DNCR industry guide gives the calling hours; check for updates before use.

Public listings do not by themselves permit contact. The OAIC says public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules where the Privacy Act applies. Coverage for a small business depends on turnover and other factors, and was not confirmed.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added.
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen.
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned.
summary: Define the properties and booking patterns you want before you look for them.
Use business listings and council registers as signals. Never contact private hosts or guests from private information.
Gaps: council registration rules, host-level lead sources and conversion rates were not sourced.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should you contact first?
options: A single property well outside your service area, because it looks large
A property manager with several apartments inside your service area that you already visit
Any host with a website, because they probably spend money on cleaning

knowledgeChecks.question: A private individual lists one holiday flat on a booking page. Which approach fits the lesson?
options: Use the guest's or the host's personal details to make contact
Leave the private host alone, and use only published business contact details
Phone the host with no check of the Do Not Call Register

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a property manager, what must you do?
options: Confirm the consent and unsubscribe requirements in current ACMA guidance
Ask the manager to like your social page first
Make the subject line as catchy as possible

sourceReferences: business.gov.au, 'How to identify your target market', https://business.gov.au/marketing/how-to-identify-your-target-market, 24 September 2024. Supports: write one short profile for each customer segment.

ACMA, 'Spam: Industry obligations', https://www.acma.gov.au/theACMA/spam-industry-obligations, last updated 28 March 2019 (older source). Supports: marketing messages need consent; an unsubscribe must work for at least 30 days and be honoured within 5 business days; publishing a business address does not by itself permit commercial messages; buying a list does not remove the duty to show consent.

OAIC, 'Chapter 7: APP 7 direct marketing', https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/australian-privacy-principles/australian-privacy-principles-guidelines/chapter-7-app-7-direct-marketing, page modified 16 October 2023; version 1.1 dated 22 July 2019 (older source). Supports: public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules.

DataVic, 'Planning Permit Application Register' (City of Casey), https://discover.data.vic.gov.au/dataset/planning-permit-application-register, metadata published 15 November 2023, last updated 5 November 2026 as shown. Victoria. Supports: some councils publish registers of planning applications with suburb and status; check your own council's register.

ACCC, 'Misleading and high pressure unsolicited sales practices widespread', https://www.accc.gov.au/media-release/misleading-and-high-pressure-unsolicited-sales-practices-widespread, 28 July 2026. Supports: many unsolicited approaches were pressured or misleading, and many salespeople did not identify themselves.

Do Not Call Register, 'DNCR industry guide', https://www.donotcall.gov.au/media/1212/dncr-industry-guide.pdf, 2018 copyright notice (older source). Supports: telemarketing to registered numbers is limited to weekdays 9am to 8pm and Saturdays 9am to 5pm, not Sundays or public holidays; lists should be checked against the register.

ACMA, 'Avoid sending spam', https://www.acma.gov.au/avoid-sending-spam, no date shown; read 2026-11-04 per the research file. Supports: consent, accurate sender details, and an unsubscribe honoured within five working days.

Business Queensland, 'Preparing a business quote: tips', https://www.business.qld.gov.au/running-business/marketing-sales/sales/preparing-quote/tips, last updated 16 November 2022. Queensland. Supports: list add-ons and alternatives on the quote; charge extra costs at cost plus a stated percentage (the source suggests 15 per cent, which is not a benchmark); follow up 7 to 14 days after the quote; confirm scope, capacity and deadline before quoting.

Notes: the City of Port Phillip accommodation register is named in the research but was not checked in detail, so it is not cited as a rule. The DNCR hours are from a 2018 guide. The short-stay example is illustrative.

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam (ACMA)
officialReferences.covers: As recorded in the research files: consent is needed before marketing messages are sent; sender details must be accurate; each commercial message needs an unsubscribe that is honoured within five working days. Publisher: ACMA.
